title: Hosted API Ephemeral Headroom Exhaustion — timeline, RCA, interim runbook
summary: On 2026-11-27 between 15:22 and 16:10 UTC we experienced a P0 degradation of the Hosted API characterized by abrupt p95 token-latency increases and elevated streaming 5xx rates. Customer-facing symptoms included stalled streams, reconnects, and an increased rate of client-side timeouts. The root cause was an ephemeral GPU pool headroom exhaustion combined with a cascade triggered by KV cache thrashing and an aggressive autoscaler cooldown misconfiguration. This doc contains a timeline, RCA, immediate mitigations taken during the incident, and an interim runbook to reduce blast radius until long-term fixes are deployed.
impact: Duration ~48 minutes of visible customer impact. ~18% of streaming sessions experienced at least one reconnect; overall 5xx rate for streaming endpoints jumped from 0.7% baseline to 12% at peak. p95 token latency for text generation rose from ~140ms to ~920ms. Several mid-market customers reported higher error rates in production; SOC on-call engaged to surface major account escalations. No data loss or unauthorized access detected.
detection: Automated synthetic monitors for streaming SLA alerted at 15:23 UTC (p95 > 500ms). On-call pager fired for hosted-api-streaming-error-rate at 15:25 UTC. Engineers began triage immediately after Slack pager. Correlated telemetry from edge-proxy, acceptor queues, and GPU telemetry indicated an in-region capacity pressure event.
timeline: 15:20 UTC — small burst of traffic from a customer bulk job hits ap-southeast region; 15:22 UTC — first synthetic alerts for elevated p95; 15:23 UTC — streaming error rate alert and page; 15:24 UTC — ops join, quick check shows host-level CPU and acceptor queue growth; 15:26 UTC — autoscaler attempted scale-up but failed to provision extra ephemeral GPUs due to soft headroom guard (min-headroom policy set too low); 15:29 UTC — KV cache eviction rate spikes as many new prefixes are seen, increasing CPU and memory pressure in serving runtime; 15:33 UTC — streaming sessions begin to fragment and fail, client reconnect storms amplify load; 15:36 UTC — SRE temporarily increased min capacity in affected pool and toggled circuit-breaker threshold to reject large multiplexed requests; 15:40 UTC — acceptor backpressure reduced, reconnect storm subsides; 16:10 UTC — metrics returned to baseline; 16:20 UTC — monitoring signaled stable; 16:45 UTC — post-incident coordination call scheduled.
root_cause: Primary: autoscaler headroom guard and scaling policy did not reserve adequate ephemeral headroom for short token-burst workloads, causing a late/incomplete scale-up. Secondary: KV cache eviction thrash caused by a surge of new prefixes increased CPU and memory pressure on the runtime, exacerbating queueing in acceptor threads and increasing token-latency. Tertiary: client reconnect behavior (no backoff) amplified load as failing streams retried aggressively, creating a feedback loop. Contributing configuration: the ephemeral pool had a cooldown value that prevented rapid burst scaling, and a recent change to packing heuristics reduced conservative pre-warming.
immediate_mitigation: 1) Increased min replicas for affected ephemeral GPU pool from 2 to 6 (manual override). 2) Temporarily relaxed autoscaler headroom guard to allow faster acquisitions. 3) Engaged edge-proxy to apply a temporary reject rule for very large multiplexed requests and enabled early failure for backpressured sessions. 4) Tuned KV cache behavior to avoid aggressive full-eviction (increased shard cache size and slowed eviction scoring). 5) Contacted major impacted customers and opened support tickets for replay/compensation where needed.
long_term_actions: - Implement predictive burst autoscaling: feed short-term rate spike predictions (1–5m) to autoscaler. - Add token-burst safe-headroom knob to pool configs with per-customer override. - Add prefix-entropy detector that pre-warms KV cache for high-variance prefixes. - Introduce client-side recommended backoff headers and update SDKs to exponential backoff on streaming reconnects. - Lower autoscaler cooldown for ephemeral pools and add fast-path scale-up flow that bypasses soft headroom when telemetry indicates hard pressure. - Add an acceptance test that simulates reconnect storms and validates circuit-breaker behavior.
runbook_playbook: Runbook (interim): 1) On streaming-error-rate pager: immediately check pool headroom and autoscaler events for affected region. 2) If headroom < configured burst threshold, manually raise min-replicas and disable headroom guard for 10 minutes. 3) Apply edge-proxy temporary reject rule for multiplexed requests > X tokens or > Y concurrent streams. 4) If KV eviction rate > 2000 evictions/min, increase cache_shard_size by +20% and disable full-eviction sampling for 15 minutes. 5) Monitor acceptor queue length and CPU; if acceptor queue > 50, enable circuit-breaker 0.7 (reject new sessions) and notify product to throttle bulk-uploads. 6) After stabilization, roll back manual overrides gradually, keeping telemetry in watch mode for 30 minutes.
metrics_snapshot: Baseline p95 token-latency: 140ms. Peak p95 during incident: 920ms. Baseline streaming 5xx: 0.7%. Peak streaming 5xx: 12%. Affected sessions: ~18% of active streaming sessions in ap-southeast. Autoscaler failure: 3 attempted scaleups failed within 3 minutes due to headroom guard. KV cache eviction rate baseline 420 evictions/min -> peaked 3,200 evictions/min.
postmortem_notes: Lessons learned: - Ephemeral pools are cost-optimized for steady-state but must have explicit tuning for short spikes; we under-indexed burst behavior. - Telemetry gaps: we lacked short-window pre-scale telemetry surfaced to paging; alerts fired too late. - Client behavior matters: users without backoff can turn transient failures into system-level events. Next steps: prioritize the predictive autoscaler work and SDK backoff rollout before Q1 2027. Consider a 'burst-safe' configuration template for customer onboarding.
